article_text:
Films and events

Cult

The Unknown

L’Inconnue

Mesmerising, stimulating and unsettling, Niels Schneider and Léa Seydoux star in this body-swap tale that grapples with the existential implications of being trapped inside someone else’s physical being.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Arthur Harari

Screenwriters Arthur Harari, Lucas Harari, Vincent Poymiro

With Léa Seydoux, Niels Schneider

France 2025. 140min

Courtesy of Pathé Films

Language French With English subtitles

Introduction

David, a withdrawn photographer, meets a mysterious woman at a party. The two share a sexual encounter, only for David to wake up the morning after in the woman’s body. Arthur Harari’s (co-writer of Anatomy of a Fall) vertiginous, occasionally harrowing and ultimately rewarding ride eschews straightforward resolution in favour of a reflection on the aftermath of severing the link between body and mind.

Diana Cipriano

With thanks to Unifrance.

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury, nudity, sex, and suicide.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Blood Countess

Isabelle Huppert dazzles as the Blood Countess in this delightful and high-camp gothic fantasy from visionary filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger.

Rogue Trooper

Duncan Jones brings the beloved 2000 AD comic strip to life with an all-guns-blazing sci-fi animation, about a soldier in a dystopian future who is sent on an impossible mission.

Nightborn

A couple’s dream of idyllic family life in the Finnish woods is shattered by the arrival of their nightmarish new baby, in Hanna Bergholm’s riotously gory folk horror.

article_text:
“ You Can See Everything ,” A24’s buzzy documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has narrowly defeated Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “ Clayface ” at the domestic box office . It added $10.6 million to bring its haul to $63.9 million. That was good enough for a first-place finish, something that “You Can See Everything” pulled off for the first time in its third weekend of release.

“Clayface,” a body horror “Batman” spinoff, earned $10.4 million, bringing its North American gross to $44.1 million. The superhero adventure has earned $83 million globally. It cost $44 million to produce, a relatively inexpensive figure for a comic book adventure. The film is part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s efforts to revitalize DC and make it a true competitor to Marvel. The duo’s first film, “Superman,” was a hit when it debuted in 2025, but “Supergirl” lost tens of millions and was excoriated by critics last summer.

Laika’s stop-motion film “Wildwood” earned $7.5 million to push its domestic total to $25 million and its global gross to $35 million. The film is adored by critics but carries a $100 million price tag, which means it will struggle to climb into the black.

Black Bear’s erotic dramedy “Wicker” earned $4.1 million from 2,374 theaters in its second weekend to push its domestic tally to $13.2 million. The studio bought the film out of Sundance for $2.5 million, so it stands to be a modest hit for the company as it gets into distributing its own movies.

Elsewhere, “Everest: The Other Side,” the new documentary from the “Free Solo” team of Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, debuted in limited release with $1 million from 515 locations. National Geographic Documentary Films backed the picture, which is expected to be an awards contender. Another Oscar hopeful, Sony Pictures Classics’ “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” expanded its footprint this weekend, earning just over $1.9 million from 1,112 screens. That brings its domestic haul to just over $2.1 million. The indie studio is pushing John Turturro for a long-overdue Academy Award nomination.

After this weekend, “You Can See Everything” has supplanted Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” to become the 18th highest-grossing documentary of all time. It cost a mere $7 million to produce.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Wayfarer Studios , Familiar Stranger and Amanat Films have set coming-of-age feature drama The Alchemy of Being Okay with Yasmeen Fletcher ( Ms. Marvel ), alongside Cherien Dabis ( All That’s Left Of You, Mo, Fallout ), Ibrahim Renno ( The Chosen, Law and Order: Organized Crime), Abubakr Ali ( Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, House of Dynamite ), Justin Chambers ( Grey’s Anatomy , The Offer ) and Abby Elliott ( All Her Fault, The Bear ).

In the aftermath of a tragedy, 17-year-old Nora (Fletcher) is desperate to escape her Midwestern life for college and the promise of New York City. As her mother Amina (Dabis) struggles to keep the family together and her father, Bassam (Renno), a gifted writer, battles demons of his own, Nora is pulled between charming classmate Qas (Ali), Mac (Chambers), an enigmatic friend of her father’s, and the teacher (Elliott) who once encouraged her writing. But as grief, family pressures and an impulsive decision collide, her carefully imagined future begins to unravel.

The project reps the feature directorial debut of Detroit native Sarah Mokh who is helming off her screenplay. She developed the original script in the 2024 Sundance Screenwriter’s Intensive and the 2024 Sundance x Disney Artist Accelerator Fellowship under the title Diary of a Muslim Cynic . The script also received support from the 2024 Gotham Week Project Market and the Hamptons International Film Festival Screenwriting Lab. The film expands on her short film debut, Cigarettes , which premiered at the 2025 SXSW Film & TV Festival. Mokh is a graduate of Harvard University and a PhD candidate at NYU.

Watch on Deadline

The film is produced by Ahmed Musiol Kolacek for Familiar Stranger, Abubakar Khan for Amanat Films, and Justin Baldoni and Andrew Calof for Wayfarer Studios. Steve Sarowitz, Jamey Heath, Angela Cardon and John Logan Pierson executive produced for Wayfarer Studios, alongside Kyle Behling. Wayfarer Studios financed the film, and UTA Independent Film Group is representing the film for domestic sales.

“The film grew out of questions I was asking myself in my early twenties about fate, responsibility, grief and whether the contours of a life are inevitable,” said Mokh. “I wanted to explore those questions through a coming-of-age story about a girl whose existential inquiries are inseparable from her anxiety about the state of the world and her inner sadness. Like, ‘is there something wrong with me, am I crazy, or is it AI and climate change or is it a family curse?’ I wanted to write a film that centered big, theological questions but was also youthful and current and honest.”

“Sarah has an extraordinary confidence and courage as a filmmaker to trust the complexity of her characters,” said Kolacek. “She allows Nora to be brilliant yet frustrating, funny yet deeply wounded, certain yet completely lost. Supporting her as she brings the ensemble to life with this exceptional cast has been incredibly rewarding, as they have uncovered so much more depth and humanity to this story than we ever could have imagined. As a filmmaker, you are always looking for that special project that feels both deeply personal and genuinely distinctive; The Alchemy of Being Okay is one of those rare films that will connect just as deeply with discerning cinephiles as it will with anyone who has ever struggled to find their way through grief and uncertainty.”

“Sarah wrote an incredibly relatable and compelling story about grief, first love and figuring out who you’re going to be, told through a distinctly diasporic lens,” said Khan. “Through my work helping bring The Glassworker and Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother to audiences, I saw that our community isn’t the ceiling of an audience. It’s where the audience starts. That’s why I want to make stories that are deeply rooted in our experiences and still have the power to travel far beyond them. The Alchemy of Being Okay is one of them”.

“Wayfarer is committed to championing emerging filmmakers with distinctive voices,” said Jamey Heath, Executive Producer and CEO of Wayfarer Studios. “Sarah is exactly that kind of filmmaker. The Alchemy of Being Okay takes an intimate and deeply personal look at grief, family and the complicated journey of growing up. We’re proud to support Sarah’s vision and bring this remarkable film to audiences.”

Mokh is represented by Simon Hurdon at Curate. Yasmeen Fletcher is represented by Authentic Talent and Literary Management, Play Management and The Gersh Agency. Dabis is represented by CAA, Strand Entertainment and Peikoff Mahan. Ali is represented by Gersh, Authentic Talent and Literary Management and Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman. Renno is represented by Venture Entertainment Partners. Chambers is represented by Gersh, Anonymous Content and Jackoway Austen Tyerman Wertheimer Mandelbaum Morris Bernstein Trattner Auerbach Hynick Jaime LeVine Sample & Klein. Elliott is represented by Paradigm and OPE Partners.

article_text:
Sofia Coppola ’s cult classic “ Marie Antoinette ” and three works by Louis Daquin , a champion of the Communist Resistance during the German occupation, are among the latest restored works from French studio Pathé .

The company, whose owners Jérôme Seydoux and Sophie Seydoux are being honored at the Lumière Film Festival ’s International Classic Film Market ( MIFC ) in Lyon, is celebrating its 130th anniversary this year, which also marks the 20th anniversary of the Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Fondation.

Related Stories

Tokyo Festival’s Women’s Empowerment Lineup Follows Those Who 'Fall Through the Cracks'

Cynthia Erivo Imagines Competing on 'The Great British Bake Off' in 'SNL U.K.' Opening Monologue: 'I've Got a Soggy Bottom and I'm Freaking Stressed!'

A bastion of film preservation and the continued transmission of heritage works, Pathé has also been a strong supporter of the Lumière Festival since its establishment in 2009.

Popular on Variety

The studio is currently marking the 20th anniversary of Coppola’s film with the release of a newly restored 4K version on Nov. 25.

The film, which stars Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman, comes just in time for the recently announced special exhibition at the Chateau de Versailles dedicated to the movie.

The 4K restoration is being supervised by Sony Pictures Entertainment in collaboration with American Zoetrope. It follows the late Eleanor Coppola’s new documentary on her daughter’s film, “ Making Marie Antoinette .”

Pathé is also celebrating the work of Daquin, described by the Lumière Festival as “a unique figure in French cinema, for whom filmmaking and political commitment were one and the same. A member of the Resistance, a staunch communist and union activist heavily involved in defending film industry workers, he considered his craft to be an extension of his convictions.”

Part of a special Lumière Festival showcase, Daquin’s works include his 1941 film “Nous les gosses”(“Portrait of Innocence”), the story of a close-knit group of schoolchildren that can be read as a veiled call for resistance. The fest is presenting the film in its restored 2K version.

Likewise screening is 1960’s “The Opportunists” (“Les Arrivistes”), an adaptation of Honoré de Balzac’s book “La Rabouilleuse” (known in English as “The Black Sheep” and “The Two Brothers”); set during the Restoration, it follows a former officer of Napoleon whose greed knows no bounds.

The Lumière Festival will present the film in its restored 4K version.

Also in the Pathé catalogue is the 4K restoration of Daquin’s 1944 drama “Premier de Cordée” (“First in Line”). Filmed primarily on location in the Chamonix Valley, “Premier de Cordée” represented a remarkable technical achievement during the German occupation of France, Pathé notes.

“Directed by a filmmaker involved in the Resistance, the film tells the story of a young man who must overcome his fear of heights to become a mountain guide. Its themes of struggle, perseverance and self-transcendence resonated strongly with audiences in occupied France.”

Pathé describes the Daquin showcase as “an opportunity to rediscover a filmmaker who captured working-class France, made films under the very nose of the occupying forces, and helped shape the institutions of post-war French cinema.

“Louis Daquin’s career was extraordinary. He directed several feature films during the German occupation while actively involved in the Communist Resistance. His films from this period bear the mark of this paradoxal situation: a left-wing filmmaker, involved in the Resistance, working under the constraints of a fascist regime.”

Speaking at the Pathé Bellecour theater in Lyon during the Classic Film Market on Friday, Jérôme Seydoux, chairman of Pathé, and Sophie Seydoux, president of the Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Fondation, discussed a wide range of pressing issues, from their efforts to preserve, conserve and transmit the company’s century-long heritage to the resilience of cinema, the undeniable power of blockbusters, and the importance of education in cultivating a lasting passion for cinema among young people.

Pathé has produced such recent upscale blockbusters as “ De Gaulle: Résistance ,” “ The Count of Monte Cristo ” and “ The Three Musketeers – Part I: D’Artagnan ” — the kinds of films that are necessary to keep cinema alive, according to Jérôme Seydoux.

“It is essential that there are films that are called locomotives in France, which Americans call blockbusters. We at Pathé said to ourselves that we are not going to make cars, we are going to make locomotives. But it’s difficult. It’s difficult because these are obviously bigger risks. These are often bigger budgets. So, you can’t make too many mistakes.”

Citing a motto from filmmaker Claude Berri, Jérôme Seydoux added, “When making a film, what matters is not what it costs, it’s what it brings in.”

Expressing his confidence in the survival of cinema, the Pathé chairman argued that despite recurring economic crises, technological shifts and the rise of home viewing, people would always seek the shared emotional experience of the big screen.

“That cinema is something that would disappear has been said since the Lumière Brothers. The Lumière Brothers, Jean-Pierre Melville, the head of Netflix, and more recently, Sylvester Stallone have announced that the cinema does not exist anymore.

“Cinema will resist, no matter what happens,” he stressed. “Cinema has always had crises. There will always be cinema, there will always be crises. And why will there always be cinema? Because today, in a society where people are very individualistic, they still have, at some point, the need to come together, to share emotions together. I am an absolutely unshakeable believer in the survival of cinema.”

Cinema will not only resist the dominance of U.S. streamers in France, it is sure to become a significant venue for platforms to launch their productions, Jérôme Seydoux added. The U.S. streamers are also natural partners for Pathé, he stressed.

“Today in France, the two main networks for the French are YouTube and Netflix. So these are two American companies. And we are going to work almost automatically with people who have money. The people who have money are the platforms. So yes, we will definitely work with the platforms. It’s mandatory.”

At the same time, Netflix will increasingly release films in theaters, he predicted. “I think they will discover that they need, what I call high fashion. When you are in the media business, you need something that shines.” For that reason, “in a short time, in a few years Netflix will make movies that will be released in theaters.”

“Not just because of the talents involved, but also for commercial reasons, for reasons that if you want to do something that is truly an event, it is difficult to make an event only on television. It will always be an event whose notoriety will be lower than that of a major film event.”

Turning to the company’s film preservation efforts and the use of digital technology, Sophie Seydoux stressed the importance of maintaining film on film.

“I am an unconditional supporter of what is called a conservation shoot, meaning that once we have restored a film, digitized it, it goes back to film. We know from here at the Lumière Festival, everywhere in the world, film is preserved for 120 years in an absolutely remarkable way. Currently, for everything that is digital, we do not know the preservation time. And above all, there are a lot of elements that can disappear overnight due to a change in technology. So, we need to be very, very careful.

“At Pathé, it’s really a golden rule. We reprint on film for all the restorations we do. There is never the slightest shadow of hesitation about it.”

Sophie Seydoux also underscored the importance of education and exposing children to films from an early age to cultivate a lasting passion for cinema. The Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Foundation conducts specialized educational workshops centered around silent films.

“It is very, very, very important to show young people films from early childhood because it will give them this desire to continue to see films,” she said. “At the Foundation we have a very, very important educational program that is focused on silent films, since that is our specialty. We teach them what film is, we let them handle film. Handling is something that is very important.

“[Company founder] Charles Pathé was very attached to everything that was manipulation. He thought about it when he built a camera, about the cameraman’s gestures, how it should be done, how it could be improved. And manipulation is very important, so many of our workshops for children involve hands-on activities.”

article_text:
Von Lintel Gallery presents When Time Played Along , the first exhibition at the gallery by Bahar Kural . In When Time Played Along , Bahar Kural reimagines the lightness of youth through the language of abstraction. The skies, seas, and shores of memory dissolve into bands of pure color — yellow, coral, turquoise — each one an emotion rather than a place, expressing how a day once felt rather than how it appeared.

By flattening the sky, mountains and sea into pure pigment, she strips away the familiar markers of place and time. Youth is remembered through the prism of time: heightened, simplified, and unreal in its perfection.

This series continues Kural’s search for what lies between photography and painting, reality and reverie. The youth remain real and unguarded, alive with sunlit gesture — but the world around them becomes stylized and symbolic. It’s as if the emotional memory of the scene has overtaken the physical one. This tension between photographic realism and painterly abstraction mirrors how we actually recall childhood — some fragments vivid, others blurred or re-colored by time.

Kural is a New York- and Istanbul-based artist.

article_text:
Going into second round of Brazil’s elections, Oliver Basciano reads the writing on the wall – for the nation’s culture industry, workers’ rights and social justice at large

It is a curiosity of São Paulo that all major protests and rallies in the city converge on its museum of art. While this is a product of urbanism and practicality – the great hulking red pillars of the Museu de Arte de São Paulo (MASP) stand smack in the middle of Avenida Paulista; the undercroft that raises the galleries from street level allows the crowd to swell into the space – it nonetheless feels symbolic: so many political battles in Brazil are fought over different visions of what defines the country’s ‘culture’.

This past Saturday, the thousands who stretched the length of the city’s most important thoroughfare, and who I later followed as they marched downtown to Praça Republica, were bedecked in the colours of the Workers’ Party (PT), as if to match MASP’s distinctive red exterior. The rally was the last stop in incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection tour. Chants of Olê, olê, olê, olá, Lu-la, Lu-la reverberated far beyond the art institution as the three-time president and veteran leftist climbed onto a float to make his election-eve speech. By the following evening, the celebrations had turned sour.

As the numbers on the electronic voting machines, from the Amazon to Pampas plains of the south, were tallied, a new reality began to take shape: the far-right, Donald Trump-backed Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair (currently jailed for attempting to orchestrate a coup upon being ousted in 2022) had won 47 percent of the vote against Lula’s 45 percent. The margin between the two in the bellwether central mining-state of Minas Gerais was even greater (voting is mandatory, but 21 percent of voters nationally abstained). Flávio and Lula will now go to a second round in three weeks’ time, but the situation for the left – and with them those invested in indigenous rights and land demarcation, the rights of LGBTQ Brazilians and Brazilian economic independence from the US – is grave.

The arts matter little in competition with such existential issues, but the diverging cultural priorities of the two candidates is emblematic of their wider attitudes towards social justice and workers’ rights. The Flávio campaign has been curiously muted about culture, with none of the rallying against ‘big time’ artists that Jair made prior to his election. For the dictatorship-romanticising Bolsonaro patriarch, culture wars were a calling card: back in 2018 there was barely a week in which I wasn’t reporting on an exhibition picketed by his supporters, artists receiving death threats or a theatre production branded parasitic on the Brazilian taxpayer. For the former army man, such attacks constituted an appeal to the powerful evangelical Christian vote and an easy foil against the metropolitan elite. There have been moments recently when I thought this kind of rubbish would return: in June a politician from Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party tried to kick up a stink about the works by La Chola Poblete, a queer indigenous artist currently showing at MASP (the sexually explicit drawings invoke Christianity). But the protest fizzled out, and Flávio’s campaign did not make much of an effort to amplify it.

In Junior’s manifesto, the arts are afforded a mere two paragraphs of beige copy, with no concrete promises, other than to look after ‘historical heritage’ without ‘subordinating it to political agendas’. With a tired electorate, the backing of Trump – whose politically motivated, crippling tariffs against Brazil have been championed by younger brother Eduardo Bolsonaro and his MAGA circle in the US – plus Flávio’s links to Rio de Janeiro’s militias (organised crime groups made up of current and former police officers), he doesn’t need to resort to such small-fry tactics. Where his father closed the Ministry of Culture with a flourish on day two of his presidency, the son is more likely to kill the arts through neglect.

Until Saturday – too late – the major problem with Lula’s campaign had been a failure to energise the wider base: PT supporters who might spread the word to their cousins and coworkers, mothers and manicurists. There’s an ageing nub that still goes out on his behalf, hands out leaflets and organises rallies all year round, but sectors like the artworld have done little to engage this time around.

A key manifesto pledge for Lula this time around has also been the 6×1 constitutional amendment bill – introduced by veteran PT deputy Reginaldo Lopes and fellow leftwinger Erika Hilton (a PSOL party deputy, she is also one of the most prominent transgender political figures in Latin America), in which the standard weekly working hours would be reduced from the current six consecutive days and just one day of rest, to five with a mandated two paid rest days a week. Flávio and his colleagues have consistently voted against the bill, and this basic bit of civilisation is certain to be killed if the right wins the second round of the elections. The 6×1 amendment would obviously be of benefit to all employees, including those working in the precarity of the culture industry, but it has obvious merits for any aspiring artist from a working-class background: a weekend that affords time to study, to practise, to rest.

In Brazil, art was long the sport of the elite. Successive Lula governments did a huge amount to widen the game, however, from the local scrappy DIY ‘culture points’ instituted by his 2000s minister of culture, the singer Gilberto Gil, to the current initiative by Margareth Menezes, the incumbent in the department (also a singer), which brings substantial arts funding to the country’s favelas. Perhaps even more important than those banner arts policies, however, has been Lula’s long-term support for public education, through which artists from a much wider base have emerged: compare this to Jair’s commitment to cut all public universities and federal institutes by 30 percent, with particular emphasis on subjects Flávio’s father declared to be ‘communist’.

On Saturday’s march, I ran into the artist Carolina Cordeiro with her daughter, the latter toddling along with a red balloon in support of Lula. Born in 1983 and one of the most conceptually rigorous Brazilian artists of her generation, Cordeiro is soon to have an exhibition at Pinacoteca de São Paulo, channelling a practice honed via a BA, an MA and a PhD all taken at public universities. There are countless other examples of artists, all of them children of PT, who widen the demographic of who gets to show in Brazilian galleries and museums beyond the oligarchic offspring of previous times. Sort life out on the ground, create the opportunities and elite institutions like galleries and museums will benefit.

If, come the 25 October second round, the left can’t recover, Lula’s trickle-up economics will be replaced by Flávio’s nepo authoritarianism. And it won’t just be artists and artworkers who suffer.

This article was updated 16 October to remove a factual inaccuracy.

article_text:
A slew of horror and genre stars are set to present at this year’s Fangoria Chainsaw Awards.

Lin Shaye (“Insidious”), Mink Stole (“Pink Flamingos”), John Kassir (“Tales from the Crypt”), Mick Garris (“Masters of Horror”), Peaches Christ, Felissa Rose (“Sleepaway Camp”), Kelli Maroney (“Night of the Comet”), Tracie Thoms (“Death Proof”) and Patrick Brice (“Creep”) are among the presenters revealed to give awards out during this year’s ceremony.

Related Stories

How to Watch MLB World Series 2026: Tampa Bay Rays vs. Milwaukee Brewers Online for Free

Fox and Endemol Shine Team to Adapt 'Fear Factor' as a Scripted Microdrama Series for My Drama App

Devon Sawa (“Final Destination,” “Chucky”) is set to host the ceremony, which will also include appearances from makeup effects legend Rick Baker, Dee Wallace (“Cujo”), James A. Janisse of Dead Meat and Biqtch Puddin’.

“28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” and “Dust Bunny” are tied for top honors with nine nominations each, followed by “Backrooms” with six nods.

The show is written and directed by Michael Varrati.

The 2026 Fangoria Chainsaw Awards will air on Oct. 25 at 9 p.m. ET on Shudder. article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Milo Manheim , the 25-year-old L.A. native recently tapped to co-lead Disney’s live-action Tangled , has landed a lead role in Michael Showalter’s redo of rom-com Serendipity for Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax .

No word yet on the role Manheim will play. We announced the project in August; Showalter described this as not a straight remake or reboot of Serendipity , but rather a contemporary “rebuttal” of the original film centered on new characters.

Written by the original’s Marc Klein, the new Serendipity will be produced by Showalter and Jordana Mollick for Semi-Formal Productions, alongside Simon Fields, who produced the original. Jonathan Glickman, Alexandra Loewy, and Thom Zadra are exec producing for Miramax, alongside Klein.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Steve Stark's Toluca Pictures Extends MGM TV Overall Deal, Expands Amazon MGM Studios First-Look Pact & Taps Max Kisbye As President

'Project Hail Mary' DoP Greig Fraser Says The Film Was The "Most Complicated" He's Ever Shot - Contenders London

Emily Crook is overseeing the project for Semi-Formal, which is under a multi-year, first-look film deal with Amazon MGM, while Arianna D’Andrea will oversee for Miramax.

Directed by Peter Chelsom and starring John Cusack and Kate Beckinsale, 2001’s Serendipity centers on a couple of strangers who fall for each other one Christmas night in New York, despite being engaged to other people. Separating, their potential future together is left unresolved — until, seven years later, each begins searching for the other.

Miramax released the film to major success — a worldwide gross exceeding $77 million — at a much different moment for the rom-com. Peter Abrams, Robert L. Levy and Simon Fields produced.

No word yet on whether the new take will be for theaters or streaming. But the original just celebrated its 25th anniversary with a screening at Wollman Rink, the Central Park ice skating venue that played a memorable supporting role.

Recently seen starring in the Paramount+ series School Spirits and Eli Roth’s horror flick Thanksgiving , Manheim is among the latest crop of young talents emerging from the world of Disney Channel to lead major studio projects. He’s best known for starring in their Zombies franchise, having also taken on roles in the likes of Prom Pact , Doogie Kameāloha, M.D. , and Camp Rock 3 .

Manheim remains in the Disney family today, as he’s currently set to star opposite Teagan Croft, in the lead role of charming thief Flynn Rider, in the studio’s live-action Tangled , heading to theaters on March 31, 2028. He is repped by Framework Entertainment, CAA, and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

editorial_title_zh: 以狂欢节作为嘲弄国王的通行证——对话阿加·雷穆什卡
editorial_excerpt_zh: 阿加·雷穆什卡（Aga Rymuszka）是 2026 年布宁-布龙格斯奖（Buning Brongers Prijzen）的六位获奖者之一。今年《Mister Motley》将采访所有这些艺术家。罗米·戴·温克尔（Romy Day Winkel）在阿加的工作室里采访了她。“我一直对荒诞主义哲学抱有兴趣：人类存在的无意义、缺乏目的……

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那个告诉她赢得了布宁-布龙格斯奖的电话打来时，距离阿加·雷穆什卡的毕业展开幕仅有一天。当时她正在拖地，第一批参观者马上就要到了。虽然当时还不能公开这个消息，但她可以告诉家人和朋友。带着满满的自信，她迎来了展览的开幕。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿加·雷穆什卡出生于华沙，毕业于海牙皇家艺术学院（KABK）。她从事大尺幅作品创作，毕业后这随即带来了一个现实问题：在海牙和鹿特丹这样的大城市里，拥有一个能让自己退后几米审视画作的独立工作室既昂贵又稀缺。目前，她在一间与女性朋友合租的工作室里画画，并在海牙皇家艺术学院的车间里制作陶瓷。她小时候曾在儿童剧团演过戏。到了青少年时期，她转向了视觉艺术，但并非一帆风顺；她首先在弗罗茨瓦夫为戏剧设计专业做准备，制作模型、观看演出、阅读关于戏剧的书籍。她被录取了，但最终还是决定离开这个国家，转而学习视觉艺术。正如她自己所说，在戏剧制作中，她主要从事执行工作，是集体机器的一部分。她真正想要的是拥有自己的艺术实践。她对戏剧的热爱依然存在，因此来自那个世界的木偶和人偶慢慢地开始出现在她的画作中。她视觉语言的其他部分也指向了这些：马戏团、狂欢节、巡回剧团。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雷穆什卡不仅在荷兰求学。在继续前往海牙之前，她曾前往西班牙交流，并在意大利生活了一年。她注意到每个国家都有其独特的艺术流派：在意大利，贫穷艺术（arte povera）的影响依然清晰可感；在西班牙是超现实主义；而在荷兰，则主要是观念艺术和抽象艺术。她说自己有意识地与潮流保持距离，但同时也承认这几乎是不可能的。在西班牙时，她大量使用明亮的色彩；自从回到荷兰后，她的调色板变得更加偏向棕色。半开玩笑地，她将此归咎于荷兰的光线、天气以及她整体的心情。在寻找鼓舞人心的视觉素材时，她也深受其物理环境的影响。她使用庞大的现成照片档案：书籍、相册、旧报纸、木偶戏和马戏团的影像，以及家庭照片。在巴塞罗那交流期间，她买了一本老旧的滑稽杂耍（burlesk）照片集，并以此创作了一段时间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_0-1024x988.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "untitled, oil on cotton canvas, 290 x 338 cm, 2025", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_1-608x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在工作室中", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的一天从阅读开始。她说，这能让“她的大脑开始运转”。接着，她坐在空白画布前，凝视、素描，翻找自己的参考资料。她从一个模糊的想法开始，围绕它建立一个现成视觉素材的档案，然后选择构图和人物。构图的铺陈是通过一根长木棍来完成的。然后她站上桌子，在靠墙的大画布上画出底稿。她从档案中挑选的人物在作画过程中会发生如此剧烈的变化，以至于到最后往往再也看不出究竟是哪张图片、哪个人或哪个木偶构成了最初的原型。这也是一项体力活：搬动梯子和桌子，往后退以观察远处的视觉效果，然后再爬上桌子。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的作品里充满了小丑、木偶师、狂欢节人物，有时还带着几乎阴森的暗调。这种荒诞对你意味着什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "阿加·雷穆什卡", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想这主要关乎规则的缺失。对“荒诞”最广泛的定义是任何超出既定秩序、超出社会规范的事物，因此它可以是各种各样的事物。这也是对形态的一种夸张。这个词本身就源于此：在意大利语中，“洞穴”是 grotto。有个传说称，曾经有人在意大利掉进了一个洞穴里，看到里面花朵、人和动物的画作交织在一起，因为在黑暗中很难看清一个图像在哪里结束、另一个图像从哪里开始。这种不同寻常的融合，据说是“荒诞”（grotesk）一词的来源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "洞穴的那种黑暗感，对你来说也包含在其中吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，我认为我的作品中存在一种潜在的黑暗感，带有一点轻微的阴森。但与此同时，我也觉得它非常具有嬉戏感。对我来说，这两个极端是交织在一起的。我一直对 absurdistische filosofie（荒诞主义哲学）抱有兴趣：人类存在的无意义、缺乏目的。这可能也是对我们所处时代的一种回应。荒诞被用作表现这一主题的手段，而夸张和嬉戏则是我展现这种黑暗感的‘形式’。因此，嬉戏感并没有掩盖黑暗，反而让人能够继续注视它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_4-905x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_3-602x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_2-1024x782.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在她看来，她的视觉语言充斥着各种木偶、游行队伍和狂欢节，散发着一种1920年代的氛围，这不是刻意选择的，而是自然而然形成的。她指出，我们正生活在咆哮的二十年代过去一百年后的今天，而历史往往只是在循环往复。在我们的交谈中，我想到了德国哲学家瓦尔特·本雅明。他在上世纪三十年代描述了在经济危机和战争威胁的时期，人们如何被巴洛克和装饰性风格所吸引，而不是严谨、简朴的美学。赖穆什卡在自己的作品中也认同这种现象。在我们交谈快结束时，她又补充了一些关于“狂欢节（carnaval）”这个词的看法：它源自拉丁语，大意是“放弃肉体”。狂欢节最初是四旬斋前的一个穷奢极欲的节日。这种过度在她看来直接契合了她对夸张的兴趣。从历史来看，狂欢节赋予了没有权力的人们自由，使他们能够扮成国王或嘲笑教皇而不受惩罚。这是等级制度的暂时颠倒，是存在本身之荒诞的发泄口。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_5-1024x577.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_6-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你拥有正规的学院派背景。你从中汲取了什么？你是否也必须戒掉一些东西？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在素描和绘画方面有着扎实的基础，我至今仍觉得这非常有用，但我也必须戒掉很多东西。回过头来看，我觉得我以前的作品太过于细节化、太过于完成了。而这正是我现在极力想要避免的。我运用了大量的留白，或者让作品的部分保持未完成状态，让草图依稀可见。尽管如此，我的创作过程在某种程度上依然是老派的：当画布涂上白底后，我会在开始在上面起稿之前，先把那层白色刮掉。我最喜欢买那种还能看到织线纹理的画布。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你什么时候会知道一件作品完成了？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不喜欢过度加工的作品。我很佩服那些具有这种天赋的画家：他们能感觉到一件作品什么时候刚刚好——不多不少，恰到好处。马丁·基彭贝格尔（Martin Kippenberger）我想就具备这种能力：他完成作品的方式对当时的往往出乎我的意料。我也在尝试这样做。通常我开始时会想把整块画布画得厚厚的，结果在画完草图和第一层后，留下了一大片未触碰的空白。然后我看着它，心想：其实这样就已经行了。这意味着我不能再动它了，否则它就会失去那种轻盈感。在我创作的大尺寸作品中，画面也必须有呼吸的空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她有时会被拿来与詹姆斯·恩索尔（James Ensor）和弗朗西斯·培根（Francis Bacon）作比较，尤其是与后者在创作手法上相似，因为培根也收集剪报。赖穆什卡认为这些相似之处大体上是巧合：画小丑的人自然很容易接近恩索尔；画死肉的人——就像她为毕业作品之一所做的那样——则无法避开一个延续数世纪的绘画传统，培根和多位古代大师都是其中的一部分。她自己更愿意提及像帕特·安德烈（Pat Andrea）这样她亲自结识过的艺术家，或者是格里尔·兰克顿（Greer Lankton），因为她那怪诞的纸 papier-mâché 雕塑和自画像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "赖穆什卡目前没有继续深造的打算；她想先积累更多的工作经验。她认为比起直接再次步入校园，这在日后会对她更有帮助。目前，她将继续在自己的档案中搜寻那些能够彻底重新描绘到面目全非的人物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_9-992x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aga Rymuszka is een van de zes winnaars van de Buning Brongers Prijzen 2026 . Mister Motley interviewt dit jaar alle kunstenaars. Romy Day Winkel spreekt Aga in haar atelier. ‘Ik ben altijd al aangetrokken geweest tot absurdistische filosofie: de zinloosheid van het menselijk bestaan, het ontbreken van een doel. Waarschijnlijk ook als reactie op de tijd waarin we leven. Het groteske dient als middel om dat te verbeelden en de overdrijving en speelsheid zijn de ‘vormen’ waarin ik die duisternis laat zien.’", "links": [{"text": "Buning Brongers Prijzen 2026", "url": "https://buningbrongers.nl/de-prijswinnaars-2026/"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Facebook", "links": [{"text": "Facebook", "url": "https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.mistermotley.nl/carnaval-als-vrijbrief-om-de-koning-te-bespotten-in-gesprek-met-aga-rymuszka/"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "X", "links": [{"text": "X", "url": "https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.mistermotley.nl/carnaval-als-vrijbrief-om-de-koning-te-bespotten-in-gesprek-met-aga-rymuszka/&text=Carnaval als vrijbrief om de koning te bespotten – in gesprek met Aga Rymuszka"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Linkedin", "links": [{"text": "Linkedin", "url": "https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.mistermotley.nl/carnaval-als-vrijbrief-om-de-koning-te-bespotten-in-gesprek-met-aga-rymuszka/"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Link kopiëren", "links": [{"text": "Link kopiëren", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/carnaval-als-vrijbrief-om-de-koning-te-bespotten-in-gesprek-met-aga-rymuszka/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Het telefoontje met het bericht dat ze de Buning Brongers Prijs had gewonnen, kwam een dag voordat de afstudeertentoonstelling van Aga Rymuszka opende. Ze was op dat moment de vloer aan het dweilen, vlak voor de eerste bezoekers zouden komen. Ze mocht het nieuws nog niet openbaar maken, maar wel aan familie en vrienden vertellen. Ze ging de opening in met een enorme boost van zelfvertrouwen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aga Rymuszka is geboren in Warschau en studeerde af aan de Koninklijke Academie van Beeldende Kunsten (KABK) in Den Haag. Ze werkt op groot formaat en dat blijkt na haar afstuderen meteen voor een praktisch probleem te zorgen: een eigen atelier, waarin ze een paar meter achteruit kan lopen om haar doeken te bekijken, is duur en schaars in steden als Den Haag en Rotterdam. Voorlopig schildert ze in een studio die ze deelt met een vriendin en maakt ze keramiek in de werkplaats van de KABK. Ze speelde als kind in een kindertheatergezelschap. Als tiener stapte ze over naar de beeldende kunst, maar niet meteen; ze bereidde zich eerst voor op een opleiding toneelvormgeving in Wrocław, maakte maquettes, ging naar voorstellingen, las over theater. Ze werd toegelaten, maar besloot toch te vertrekken, het land uit, om in plaats daarvan beeldende kunst te gaan studeren. In een theaterproductie is ze, zoals ze het zelf noemt, vooral uitvoerend aan het werk; onderdeel van een collectief apparaat. Wat ze echt wilde was een eigen praktijk. De liefde voor het theater bleef, waardoor de poppen en figuren uit die wereld langzaam maar zeker in haar schilderwerk begonnen op te duiken. Ook de rest van haar beeldtaal verwijst daarnaar: circus, carnaval, rondtrekkende theatergezelschappen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rymuszka studeerde niet alleen in Nederland. Ze ging voor een uitwisseling naar Spanje en woonde een jaar in Italië voordat ze in Den Haag verderging. Ze merkte dat elk land zijn eigen kunststromingen meebracht: in Italië was de invloed van arte povera nog voelbaar aanwezig, in Spanje het surrealisme en in Nederland vooral de conceptuele en abstracte kunst. Ze zegt bewust afstand te willen houden van trends, maar erkent tegelijkertijd dat dat haast onmogelijk is. In Spanje schilderde ze veel met felle kleuren, sinds ze terug is in Nederland is haar palet bruiner geworden. Ze wijt dat, half lachend, aan het licht, het weer, haar algehele stemming in Nederland. Ook bij het vinden van inspirerend beeldmateriaal wordt ze sterk door haar fysieke omgeving beïnvloed. Ze werkt met een uitgebreid archief van gevonden foto’s: boeken, albums, oude kranten, beelden van het poppentheater en het circus, maar ook familiefoto’s. article_text:
Aga Rymuszka is een van de zes winnaars van de Buning Brongers Prijzen 2026 . Mister Motley interviewt dit jaar alle kunstenaars. Romy Day Winkel spreekt Aga in haar atelier. ‘Ik ben altijd al aangetrokken geweest tot absurdistische filosofie: de zinloosheid van het menselijk bestaan, het ontbreken van een doel. Waarschijnlijk ook als reactie op de tijd waarin we leven. Het groteske dient als middel om dat te verbeelden en de overdrijving en speelsheid zijn de ‘vormen’ waarin ik die duisternis laat zien.’

Facebook

X

Linkedin

Link kopiëren

Het telefoontje met het bericht dat ze de Buning Brongers Prijs had gewonnen, kwam een dag voordat de afstudeertentoonstelling van Aga Rymuszka opende. Ze was op dat moment de vloer aan het dweilen, vlak voor de eerste bezoekers zouden komen. Ze mocht het nieuws nog niet openbaar maken, maar wel aan familie en vrienden vertellen. Ze ging de opening in met een enorme boost van zelfvertrouwen.

Aga Rymuszka is geboren in Warschau en studeerde af aan de Koninklijke Academie van Beeldende Kunsten (KABK) in Den Haag. Ze werkt op groot formaat en dat blijkt na haar afstuderen meteen voor een praktisch probleem te zorgen: een eigen atelier, waarin ze een paar meter achteruit kan lopen om haar doeken te bekijken, is duur en schaars in steden als Den Haag en Rotterdam. Voorlopig schildert ze in een studio die ze deelt met een vriendin en maakt ze keramiek in de werkplaats van de KABK. Ze speelde als kind in een kindertheatergezelschap. Als tiener stapte ze over naar de beeldende kunst, maar niet meteen; ze bereidde zich eerst voor op een opleiding toneelvormgeving in Wrocław, maakte maquettes, ging naar voorstellingen, las over theater. Ze werd toegelaten, maar besloot toch te vertrekken, het land uit, om in plaats daarvan beeldende kunst te gaan studeren. In een theaterproductie is ze, zoals ze het zelf noemt, vooral uitvoerend aan het werk; onderdeel van een collectief apparaat. Wat ze echt wilde was een eigen praktijk. De liefde voor het theater bleef, waardoor de poppen en figuren uit die wereld langzaam maar zeker in haar schilderwerk begonnen op te duiken. Ook de rest van haar beeldtaal verwijst daarnaar: circus, carnaval, rondtrekkende theatergezelschappen.

Rymuszka studeerde niet alleen in Nederland. Ze ging voor een uitwisseling naar Spanje en woonde een jaar in Italië voordat ze in Den Haag verderging. Ze merkte dat elk land zijn eigen kunststromingen meebracht: in Italië was de invloed van arte povera nog voelbaar aanwezig, in Spanje het surrealisme en in Nederland vooral de conceptuele en abstracte kunst. Ze zegt bewust afstand te willen houden van trends, maar erkent tegelijkertijd dat dat haast onmogelijk is. In Spanje schilderde ze veel met felle kleuren, sinds ze terug is in Nederland is haar palet bruiner geworden. Ze wijt dat, half lachend, aan het licht, het weer, haar algehele stemming in Nederland. Ook bij het vinden van inspirerend beeldmateriaal wordt ze sterk door haar fysieke omgeving beïnvloed. Ze werkt met een uitgebreid archief van gevonden foto’s: boeken, albums, oude kranten, beelden van het poppentheater en het circus, maar ook familiefoto’s. Tijdens haar uitwisseling in Barcelona kocht ze een boek met oude burlesk-foto’s, waar ze een tijd lang mee werkte.

In het atelier

Haar dag begint met lezen. Daardoor beginnen, zo zegt ze, ‘haar hersenen te werken’. Dan gaat ze voor een leeg doek zitten, kijkt, schetst, doorzoekt haar referenties. Ze begint met een vaag idee, bouwt daar een dossier van gevonden beeldmateriaal omheen, kiest een compositie en figuren. Het uitzetten van die compositie gebeurt met een lange houten stok. Dan staat ze op tafel en tekent ze een opzet op een groot doek dat tegen de muur staat. De figuren die ze uit haar archief kiest, veranderen tijdens het schilderen zo drastisch, dat uiteindelijk vaak niet meer te zien is welk beeld, welke persoon of welke pop aan de basis stond. Het is ook fysiek werk: ladders en tafels verschuiven, naar achteren lopen om te zien hoe het van een afstand oogt, weer de tafel op.

Je werk zit vol clowns, poppenspelers, carnavalsfiguren, met soms een haast sinistere ondertoon. Wat betekent dat groteske voor jou?

Aga Rymuszka

Ik denk dat het vooral gaat om de afwezigheid van regels. De breedste definitie van ‘het groteske’ is alles wat buiten de gevestigde orde valt, buiten de sociale norm, en dat kan dus van alles zijn. Het is ook een overdrijving van vormen. Het woord zelf komt daaruit voort: in het Italiaans is ‘grot’ grotto . Er bestaat een verhaal dat iemand in Italië ooit in een grot viel en daar tekeningen van bloemen, mensen en dieren in elkaar over zag lopen, omdat in het donker niet goed te zien was waar het ene beeld ophield en het andere begon. Die ongewone samensmelting is waar het woord grotesk vandaan zou komen.

Die duisternis van de grot, zit die er voor jou ook in?

Ja, ik denk dat er een onderliggende duisternis in mijn werk zit, iets licht sinisters. Maar ik vind het tegelijk heel speels. Die twee uitersten zijn voor mij met elkaar verweven. Ik ben altijd al aangetrokken geweest tot absurdistische filosofie: de zinloosheid van het menselijk bestaan, het ontbreken van een doel. Waarschijnlijk ook als reactie op de tijd waarin we leven. Het groteske dient als middel om dat te verbeelden en de overdrijving en speelsheid zijn de ‘vormen’ waarin ik die duisternis laat zien. Het speelse verhult de duisternis dus niet, het maakt het juist mogelijk om ernaar te blijven kijken.

Dat haar beeldtaal met al haar poppen, optochten en het carnaval een jarentwintigsfeer ademt, is volgens haar niet bewust gekozen, maar organisch ontstaan. Ze wijst erop dat we honderd jaar na de roaring twenties leven en dat geschiedenis nu eenmaal in cirkels lijkt te bewegen. Tijdens ons gesprek moest ik denken aan de Duitse filosoof Walter Benjamin. Hij beschreef in de jaren dertig van de vorige eeuw hoe mensen in tijden van economische crisis en oorlogsdreiging worden aangetrokken tot het barokke en het ornamentele, in plaats van tot een strenge, sobere esthetiek. Rymuszka herkent dat fenomeen in haar eigen werk. Tegen het einde van ons gesprek voegt ze daar nog iets aan toe, over het woord ‘carnaval’: dat komt uit het Latijn en betekent zoiets als het ‘afstand doen van vlees’. Carnaval fungeerde in eerste instantie als een decadent feest vlak voor de vastentijd. Die overdaad sluit voor haar direct aan bij haar interesse in overdrijving. Historisch gaf het carnaval mensen zonder macht de vrijheid om zich als koning te verkleden of de paus te bespotten zonder gestraft te worden. Een tijdelijke omkering van de hiërarchie, een uitlaatklep voor het absurde van het bestaan zelf.

Je hebt een technische academische achtergrond. Wat heb je daarvan meegenomen? Moest je ook dingen afleren?

Ik heb een stevige basis in tekenen en schilderen en dat vind ik nog steeds heel bruikbaar, maar ik heb ook veel moeten afleren. Ik vind mijn werk van vroeger met terugwerkende kracht te gedetailleerd, te afgemaakt. Dat probeer ik nu juist te vermijden. Ik gebruik veel lege ruimtes, of laat delen van het werk onaf, met de schets nog zichtbaar. Toch is mijn proces op een bepaalde manier nog steeds ouderwets: als een doek wit geprepareerd is, haal ik eerst dat wit weg voordat ik erop begin te schetsen. Ik koop het liefst doeken waarvan je de draad nog kunt zien.

Wanneer weet je dat een werk af is?

Ik hou er niet van als een werk overdone is. Ik bewonder schilders die het talent hebben om te voelen wanneer een werk precies genoeg is; niet te weinig, maar ook niet te veel. Martin Kippenberger had dat volgens mij: hij maakte zijn werk op een manier af die voor mij vaak onverwacht is. Dat probeer ik ook te doen. Vaak begin ik met het idee dat ik het hele doek dik ga beschilderen en dan blijft er na de schets en een eerste laag een groot onaangeraakt vlak over. Dan kijk ik ernaar en denk ik: dit werkt eigenlijk al. Dat betekent dat ik er niet meer aan mag komen, want dan verliest het die lichtheid. Bij het grote formaat waarop ik schilder, moet een werk ook ademruimte hebben.

Ze wordt weleens vergeleken met James Ensor en Francis Bacon, met de laatste vooral qua werkwijze, omdat Bacon eveneens knipsels uit kranten verzamelde. Rymuszka ziet die overeenkomsten als grotendeels toevallig: wie clowns schildert, komt nu eenmaal snel in de buurt van Ensor; wie dood vlees schildert, zoals zij deed voor een van haar afstudeerwerken, ontkomt niet aan een eeuwenoude schildertraditie waar Bacon en verschillende oude meesters deel van uitmaken. Ze noemt zelf liever kunstenaars als Pat Andrea, die ze persoonlijk ontmoette, of Greer Lankton, vanwege haar groteske papier-maché-beelden en zelfportretten.

Een vervolgopleiding komt er voorlopig niet voor Rymuszka; ze wil eerst meer werkervaring opdoen. Ze denkt dat ze daar later meer aan zal hebben dan meteen weer in een opleiding te stappen. Voor nu blijft ze zoeken naar figuren in haar archief die ze grondig genoeg kan herschilderen om ze onherkenbaar te maken.

Over de Buning Brongers Prijzen De Buning Brongers Prijs is een Nederlandse kunstprijs voor jonge beeldend kunstenaars. De prijzen worden eens in de twee jaar uitgereikt door de Buning Brongers Stichting uit de nalatenschap van Johan Buning en zijn familie. De prijs bestaat dit jaar 60 jaar en is sinds 1966 uitgereikt aan 174 kunstenaars. Aan de prijs is een geldbedrag verbonden van € 4.500 per winnaar. De kandidaten voor de prijs zijn de afgelopen twee jaar afgestudeerd aan kunstacademies in Nederland en voorgedragen door hun academie. De prijsuitreiking en opening van de tentoonstelling van de zes winnaars vinden plaats op vrijdag 13 november in Arti et Amicitiae te Amsterdam. Je bent van harte uitgenodigd hierbij aanwezig te zijn.

Een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit in Spui 25 Voorafgaand aan de prijsuitreiking in Arti et Amicitiae organiseert de stichting een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit in Spui 25. Hans den Hartog Jager en Heske ten Cate geven elk een presentatie waarin ze dieper ingaan op hun persoonlijke ervaringen en inzichten. Aansluitend gaan Dineke Blom, Ricardo van Eyk en Robert Zandvliet met elkaar in gesprek. Je bent ook hier van harte welkom!

麦切画和自肖像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "目前,Rymuszka还没有继续学习;她首先想获得更多的工作经验;她认为她以后会有更多的努力,而不是立即重新进入培训;到目前为止,她仍然在她的档案中寻找人物,她可以充分地重新绘制,使他们不可识别。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_9-992x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/work_7-498x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于Buning Brongers 奖项 The Buning Brongers 奖项是为年轻的画家提供的荷兰艺术奖,由Johan Buning和他的家人继承的Buning Brongers 基金会每两年颁发一次。 60 一年之久,是 1966 授予 174 艺术家:价格上有钱的金额 4.500 获奖者:获奖者在过去两年中毕业于艺术学院荷兰和由他们的学院提交。 奖项提名和六名获奖者的展览的开幕式将于11月13日星期五在阿姆斯特丹的Arti et Amicitiae举行。", "links": [{"text": "De Buning Brongers Prijs", "url": "https://buningbrongers.nl/"}, {"text": "prijsuitreiking en opening van de tentoonstelling", "url": "https://buningbrongers.nl/de-prijzen/prijsuitreiking/"}, {"text": "zes winnaars", "url": "https://buningbrongers.nl/de-prijswinnaars-2026/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于艺术和质量的对话在斯皮亚25在阿提和阿米奇蒂亚奖颁奖典礼之前,该基金会在斯皮亚25举办了关于艺术和质量的对话,Hans den Hartog Jager和Heske ten Cate每个人都提供了一个介绍,他们深入了解他们的个人经历和认识。", "links": [{"text": "een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit", "url": "https://buningbrongers.nl/symposium/"}], "translated": true}]

title_original: As Art Basel Paris Shutters for Weekend Protests, Satellite Fairs Keep Their Doors Open

editorial_excerpt_zh: 以下是巴黎各地一些小型艺博会的亮点，以及它们如何应对周六计划中的抗议活动。

article_text:
If you planned to visit Art Basel Paris but just learned that it’s closing for the weekend ahead of Saturday’s planned protests, there’s some good news: for now, at least, several satellite fairs plan to welcome visitors for part or all of the weekend—while keeping an eye on the surrounding social and political context as it evolves in real time.

As of Thursday night, Asia NOW and Paris Internationale told ARTnews they are staying open as planned, through October 24, while exhibitors at OFFSCREEN said they received official confirmation that the fair will remain open through Sunday, October 25. ( OFFSCREEN organizers did not respond to a request for confirmation by the time of writing.) Outsider Paris also said it plans to stay open through Sunday, while responding to circumstances as they change.

Post-Fair , located in two neighboring buildings in the Marais, said the ongoing fair will open an hour earlier, at 10 a.m. on Saturday, and close at 1 p.m., rather than that evening. Other fairs had not responded to requests for confirmation of their weekend plans at the time of writing.

“I think that closing a few hours early is the right decision given the uncertainty,” said Robert Heald, of the eponymous gallery in Wellington, New Zealand, showing at Post-Fair. “I am very happy with how the fair has gone, and safety must come first,” he added. Heald is showing contemporary and historic works on paper by the acclaimed outsider artist Susan Te Kahurangi King, of whom the New Yorker recently wrote, “at 75, may be New Zealand’s greatest living artist.” “The works have this quite strong, visceral, bodily energy to them, which is quite interesting given the fact that she stopped speaking at the age of five,” said Heald. Works on paper range from $8,000 to $16,000.

This is Post-Fair’s inaugural Paris edition, following its 2025 founding in Los Angeles by Chris Sharp. It features 35 galleries from 15 countries and is billed as “a carefully crafted, boutique, and invitation-only alternative to the conventional art-fair model.” Galleries don’t have separate booths and instead exhibit one or two artists in open-plan layouts, with project spaces taking up as little as one wall. The two venues feel elegant and brightly lit, including a 17th-century hôtel particulier, or mansion, with vaulted stone ceilings on the bottom floor, and an Art Deco building across the Rue du Temple.

Sharp told ARTnews that the first preview day, on Monday, was “bonkers; we had almost 1,000 people.” He added, “It totally exceeded my expectations”—this, despite last weekend’s protests. “I think people in general are just so excited to be in Paris.”

He also found that collectors generally “take it slower. They want to learn more about the work, the CV, no matter what the price point, which I really appreciate, because I think they’re serious, and you know they’re not going to turn around and flip it. Take it slower, be more deliberate,” Sharp said.

Los Angeles gallery Nonaka-Hill is presenting a standout group of works by Japanese artist Sawako Goda (1940–2016), including airbrushy Pop paintings and delicate Xerox photocopy prints of fish with long-lashed eyeballs. These are shown alongside porcelain hanging “Spoon” sculptures by Japanese artist Kentaro Kawabata (born 1976), which have a marine or alien-life feeling, with skeletal as well as invertebrate components, rendered in delicious color and intricately crafted clay.

“We met amazing people who don’t regularly pass through Los Angeles and Kyoto, so it was beautifully connective,” Rodney Nonaka-Hill told ARTnews . “Sales were sufficient, and the spirit was good, despite the distraction. Art people proved intrepid.”

Elsewhere, at Paris Internationale , some dealers said their clients had promised to make it out to this edition’s new venue in the northeast part of town but had struggled to find the time. Nevertheless, most said sales had been good for the first part of the fair.

Among several other strong presentations pairing historic with contemporary works was Parker Gallery’s, which showed assembled paintings by Thornton Dial (1928–2016) and ceramic and collage crown sculptures by Bay Area artist Sahar Khoury. Prices range from $8,000 to $75,000.

New works by UK artist Aimée Parrot at Kate MacGarry gallery are another great discovery. Parrot paints onto glass or metal and transfers the prints onto cotton canvas, which she often stitches together and paints over. She is currently showing work at the Cample Line art space in Scotland. Prices range from £4,500 to £12,500.

Though protests are not expected near the Paris Internationale venue Saturday, Galerie Derouillon said it preferred to close early, on Friday night, to ensure the safety of staff and artworks as people travel home or away from the fair. Gallery director Marion Coindeau said the fair had gone well, with sales and strong interest in paintings and sculptures by Alex Foxton and Mathilde Albouy.

“We feel the majority of collectors that we’d have seen have already come by, and with Saturday’s protests, as well as the fear instilled by Art Basel closing, we don’t think many people will want to come by,” said Coindeau. She herself was stuck inside the centrally located gallery last Saturday due to tear gas and clashes with police nearby, she said. Similarly, she was concerned that staff who don’t live near the fair could find themselves unable to leave the venue by day’s end.

OFFSCREEN—like last year, located in the expansive, 17th-century Chapelle Saint-Louis de la Salpêtrière on the Left Bank, not far from the Seine—is not near the planned protests. Set on the grounds of a large hospital, it is also protected and removed from the street.

This year, the fair, dedicated to fixed and moving images, is honoring Ana Mendieta with a special presentation of her films under the grand cupola. Another must-see is brought by Galerie Max Hetzler, featuring a strange and captivating “fictional autobiographical” film titled A Life in a Day (2021–23) and a handmade mask by Rinus Van de Velde, who imagines himself traveling the world to meet artistic heroes, or behaving like the artist he wishes he were. Van de Velde also has his largest exhibition at a US institution to date, The Dinner , on view in Marfa, Texas, through December 6.

On Thursday evening, the gallery announced it had been awarded the Cultish x OFFSCREEN prize for the best artistic presentation. “It’s been really exciting being in such an incredible setting, and having this more tightly curated focus,” said a gallery representative, who echoed other exhibitors in noting that many international curators and museums had already been through the fair.

Paris Internationale, with 54 international galleries and a strong Hispanic and South Korean contingent this year, also aims for a more curated, smaller-scale, and approachable setting. “We intentionally condensed this year. It’s something we always aim for, because we think a tighter format is best—it’s not for lack of demand,” said fair director Silvia Ammon. “It’s a choice.”

article_text:
Indian superstar Rajinikanth ’s Tamil-language action comedy “ Jailer 2 ” was the second-biggest film in the world over the Oct. 16–18 weekend, grossing $31.2 million, according to Rentrak estimates. Only Paramount’s “Street Fighter,” with $51.1 million, earned more.

The Nelson Dilipkumar-directed sequel opened in India on, Oct. 15, and grossed an estimated INR224 crore ($23.5 million) across its four-day extended opening. That is the third-highest four-day start on record for a Tamil-language film, and effectively level with another Rajinikanth vehicle, “Coolie,” which managed INR224.25 crore ($23.6 million).

Related Stories

Netflix, Bengali Streamer Hoichoi Partner to Bring Series to Hindi, Tamil and Telugu Audiences

Bela Bajaria on Netflix's Epic TV Trek Into Local Language Production: 'There's No Roadmap for This'

The film began with $7 million on Thursday. Collections dipped on Friday before climbing back through the weekend, with Sunday bringing in $6.5 million.

Popular on Variety

Tamil Nadu, the southern Indian state where the Tamil-language film industry is based, delivered the biggest share at $8.4 million. The neighboring southern Indian states of Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana supplied most of the remainder.

In North America, where the film is distributed by Shloka Entertainments, “Jailer 2” grossed $3.2 million over the Friday-to-Sunday frame, debuting at No. 9, taking its total to $5.2 million. Shloka said the film crossed $2 million on its opening day in the territory.

“Jailer 2” follows the 2023 hit “Jailer,” in which Rajinikanth played a retired prison warden drawn back into violence when an idol smuggler threatens his family. He returns as “Tiger” Muthuvel Pandian, with Ramya Krishnan, Yogi Babu and Mirnaa also reprising their roles. New to the franchise are Tamil actor S.J. Suryah as Bodhi Kalpak and Bollywood star Vidya Balan as Kaantha. Veteran Bollywood actor Mithun Chakraborty and Malayalam cinema actor Suraj Venjaramoodu also join the cast. Dilipkumar wrote and directed both films for Kalanithi Maran’s Sun Pictures, and Anirudh Ravichander again composed the music.

The sequel also brings in stars from other Indian language industries for brief appearances. Malayalam cinema icon Mohanlal and Kannada star Shiva Rajkumar, both of whom made cameos in the first film, return as Mathew and Narasimha, and Bollywood veteran Jackie Shroff plays Kamdev. Hrithik Roshan turns up as Roddy. The scene reunites Roshan with Rajinikanth 40 years after the 1986 Hindi film “Bhagwan Dada,” in which Roshan appeared as a child.

Elsewhere on the global chart, Sony’s “Resident Evil” ranked third with $22.6 million, followed by Universal’s “Other Mommy” at $17.9 million and “Verity” at $17.6 million.

article_text:
神戸のアートブック書店THE BOOK ENDにて、10月8日（木）より小島康敬による写真展「中今 | ベルリン」を開催している。

写真家・小島康敬が提示するのは、私たちが知る歴史や記憶から乖離し、時空間をも通り抜けたような、どこでもない「ベルリン」。 最先端の量子理論や、時間と空間の中心を指す古神道の概念「中今（Naka-ima）」に着想を得て制作された本シリーズは、過去・現在・未来が同時に存在する「立体的な今」を静かに捉え引き出す試みだ。

東京、ニューヨークを経てたどり着いた目線の高さによる平面的でミニマルな画面構成。 特定の場所や歴史的表象を削ぎ落とした作品群は、ロラン・バルトが称した「空虚な記号」のように中心を空虚に保ち、観る者に意味の解釈をそっと委ねる。 撮影された瞬間の「かつてあった」一瞬の奥に流れる時間と距離、そしてどこか静けさを纏った円環する時間の深みを、ぜひ会場でご体験いただきたい。

タイトル

小島康敬「中今 | ベルリン」

場所

THE BOOK END（兵庫県神戸市中央区海岸通3-1-5海岸ビルヂング 302 ）

会期

2026年10月8日（木）〜11月9日（日）

時間

11:00〜18:00

休館日

火、水曜

入場料

無料

URL

https://the-book-end.com/exhibition/681/

title_original: At Frieze, an Artist Project in the Fair’s Public Toilets Confronts the UK’s Ongoing Bathroom Wars
editorial_title_zh: 在弗里兹艺博会上，展会公共卫生间内的一项艺术家项目直面英国持续不断的“卫生间之争”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 观众受邀使用格雷·维莱宾斯基（Gray Wielebinski）全新场域特定作品《Production》（2026年），其中包含带香味的男用小便池块和马桶边缘洁厕块。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在本周的伦敦弗里兹艺博会上，连洗手间也将成为欣赏艺术的场所。格雷·维莱宾斯基（Gray Wielebinski）全新场域特定作品《Production》（2026年）将把艺博会的公共卫生间改造成一个充满亲密感的嗅觉环境，气味、身体机能、隐私、欲望与监控在此交汇。", "links": [{"text": "Gray Wielebinski", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/gray-wielebinski/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Production》并没有隐没于洗手间的功能性基础设施之中，而是作为一件艺术品宣告自身的存在：定制的散发着两种气味的小便池块和马桶边缘洁厕块被放置在雕塑般的笼子里，上面还带有防盗扣。它们造型奇异、色彩鲜艳且带有香味。其中一块几乎呈口红般的红色，而另一块则是黑色的。它们的质感也与典型的小便池块不同。“它们看起来几乎像是化妆品，或者像是一种艺术材料，”他在该作品于摄政公园安装前接受《ARTnews》采访时说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "弗里兹上一次委托艺术家为其洗手间创作作品是在十年前，即朱莉·韦霍芬（Julie Verhoeven）的《The Toilet Attendant… Now Wash Your Hands》（2016年），该行为艺术作品中由艺术家本人扮演洗手间服务员。与《Production》一样，那件作品通过对艺术界劳动伦理的评述，具有了一层政治维度。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Production》与调香师 Dean’s Bottom 合作制作，其每一个独立部件都带有维莱宾斯基的名字和一个防盗扣，尽管它们不出售，但在技术上属于限量版。“这也引发了关于价值的问题，”他说，并将其与作品的整体环境——一个艺术博览会联系起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些物体的雕塑感笼子为作品增添了另一层含义，将它们与保护和排斥的观念联系在一起。对维莱宾斯基而言，洗手间是一个充满张力的特定场所，性别化空间的政治常常在那里被用来对跨性别者和性别不合规范者对洗手间的使用进行规训。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Gray-Wielebinski-Deans-Bottom-Production-Frieze-London-2026.jpg?w=400", "alt": "小便池内一个带笼子且略微使用过的小便池块。", "caption": "格雷·维莱宾斯基，《Production》，2026年，伦敦弗里兹艺博会2026年展出现场，由 Deans Bottom 呈献。图片：Linda Nylind/Frieze 供图", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在整个英国，今年8月生效的一项新的官方指导意见规定，向公众开放的单一性别空间（包括餐馆、健身房、医院病房和避难所等场所的卫生间和更衣室）应根据生理性别进行组织。该指导意见由平等与人权委员会（EHRC）发布，其中补充称，跨性别者应使用中性设施或与其生理性别相符的设施。此前，英国最高法院于2025年4月裁定，平等法中的“性”指的是“生理性别”，而非某人认同的性别。跨性别权益活动人士强烈反对该准则的实施，跨性别者+声援联盟（Trans+ article_text:
At Frieze London this week, even the bathroom will be a place to see art. Gray Wielebinski ’s new site-specific Production (2026) will transform the fair’s public toilets into an intimate olfactory environment, where scent, bodily function, privacy, desire, and surveillance will converge.

Rather than disappearing into the functional infrastructure of the bathroom, Production announces itself as an artwork: Custom urinal cakes and toilet-rim blocks infused with two scents are housed in sculptural cages, with security tags attached. They are strange, brightly colored, and scented. One is almost lipstick-red, while the other is black. Their texture is also different from typical urinal cakes. “They almost look like cosmetics, or like an art material,” he told ARTnews in an interview ahead of the work’s installation at the Regent’s Park.

The last time Frieze commissioned an artist to make work about its bathrooms was a decade ago, with Julie Verhoeven’s The Toilet Attendant… Now Wash Your Hands (2016), featuring the artist as the attendant in a piece of performance art. Like with Production , that work with its commentary on the ethics of labor in the art world, had a political dimension to it.

Made in collaboration with perfumier Dean’s Bottom, each of Production ’s individual parts carries Wielebinski’s name and a security tag, and though they are not for sale, they are, technically, editioned. “It’s bringing up questions of value too,” he said, connecting it to the work’s overall setting, an art fair.

The objects’ sculptural cages add another layer to the work, connecting them to ideas of protection and exclusion. For Wielebinski, the bathroom is a particularly charged site, where the politics of gendered space have been used to police their use by transgender and gender non-conforming people.

Across the UK, new official guidance that came into force this past August states that single-sex spaces open to the public, including toilets and changing rooms in places like restaurants, gyms, hospital wards, and refuges, should be organized based on biological sex. The guidance, published by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), adds that trans people should use either gender-neutral facilities or the ones that match their biological sex. It comes after the UK Supreme Court ruled, in April 2025, that “sex” in equality law means “biological sex” rather than the gender someone identifies as. Trans-rights activists have strongly opposed the code’s implementation, with Trans+ Solidarity Alliance calling the gudiance “unworkable.”

“I think it’s something that I’m obviously very—I don’t want to say ‘drawn to’ but it impacts my life on a daily basis,” he said. “The bathroom holds a very fraught and also sacred and fun and ambivalent place in my world, in my life, in my psyche.”

Wielebinski first became interested in using scent for his 2023 installation Exhibition for the British department store Selfridges. “It started extremely organically,” Wielebinski said, describing his current olfactory obsession as a means of creating atmosphere and a way of translating between different mediums.

The scent of Production is also intentionally familiar, especially for any artists attending Frieze. Wielebinski describes them as “a take on the industrial smelling urinal cake that already exists that we’re used to smelling in the bathroom coinciding with a more conceptual scent based off of the scents of my studio.”

Wielebinski said he wasn’t quite sure what emotion Production will elicit of those who interact with it, though he expects a “wide range of feelings,” from attraction to disgust, curiosity to ambivalence. His intention isn’t one of provocation but to provide a collective experience to an otherwise private moment, or “a hushed secret thing that then also becomes communal in whatever way that might be,” he said, adding that he hopes it become the topic of conversations, jokes, and even criticism.

“Whenever you put work out in the world, it’s out of your hands, but I also think that’s, for me, when my work comes alive, when an audience interacts with it,” he said, noting that he wants to “draw people’s attention to all these things about what a bathroom can mean, and what a body can mean.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: “当事情正在发生时，我很庆幸自己还活着，”詹姆斯·巴诺（James Barnor）说道。独立前夕的阿克拉，披头士乐队时期的伦敦：这些理由足以让他自称“幸运吉姆”（Lucky Jim）。简而言之，这是一个幸运的人（《幸运吉姆》也是金斯利·艾米斯［Kingsley Amis］于1954年出版的小说，时代不同，但调性一致）……

article_text:
“I was lucky to be alive when things were happening,” says James Barnor. Accra on the eve of independence, London in the days of the Beatles: reason enough to call himself Lucky Jim. A lucky man, in short ( Lucky Jim is also a Kingsley Amis novel, published in 1954, different era, same vein). At 97, he headlines an opening that doubles as a housewarming.

At 51, rue Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière reopens after several weeks of work. More than 250 m² (about 2,700 square feet) of exhibition space extending from the street-front bookshop, a showroom, an office dedicated to digitizing and consulting photographic collections: the back room has taken on the air of an archive reading room. The choice of guest was obvious. Since 2015, the team has worked on James Barnor’s archive, sorted and catalogued with him on site between 2017 and 2021. A long-haul loyalty.

There is a certain delight in finding James Barnor in his own pictures, the man who spent his life composing other people’s. Accra, 1952: a young father dressed all in white, straight as a rod against a whitewashed wall, he holds his son Daniel in his christening gown. That same year, on assignment for the Daily Graphic , he leans over a staircase banister, twin-lens camera in hand and saucer flash at the ready, a friend with a cigarette on his lips playing prompter. Dressed to the nines, already.

Then England. James Barnor landed in Liverpool on December 1, 1959, and worked night shifts in a factory alongside a Ghanaian boxer, Attuquaye Clottey, who thought he was mad to have left his studio. In 1960 came Dennis Kemp, a lecturer for Kodak: “Look I can offer you board and lodging but no pay,” he told him (Barnor recalled it in 2019). His friend photographed him draped in his kente, leaning on an “England” road sign in Shropshire, motorbike parked in the hedge, or seated beneath a giant “CAFÉ” sign. The ease of a prince on tour.

Back in Accra in the late 1960s, James Barnor was hired by Agfa-Gevaert to set up the country’s first color lab. There he posed an assistant among bottles of developing chemicals, pink, green, white, coral, in place of a color chart. A makeshift swatch book, mischief intact. Elsewhere, a grid of 12 frames shot at the Agfa-Gevaert laboratory in Mortsel, Belgium: he slips in beside a model in a striped top, then takes the colored backdrop alone. Self-portrait as a diligent student.

On October 22, the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain opens “Le temps des récoltes” (The Time of Harvests) by Ibrahim Mahama, which includes the “Agip” series, made for the brand’s 1974 calendar. The occasion for James Barnor’s return to Paris. “I’m lucky to be alive and to be telling the story about my work,” he says. Lucky Jim, still.

James Barnor, “Lucky Jim” is on view through November 21, 2026 at Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière , Paris.

article_text:
Issue

151 News Roundup: Controversies, Career Moves, Infrastructure, Public Domain

GAO ZHEN . Photo by and courtesy Xiao Ke.

Controversies

Chinese dissident artist Gao Zhen was sentenced to three years in prison by the Sanhe City People’s Court over sculptures of Mao Zedong he created over 15 years ago. The verdict, delivered on August 25, found Gao guilty of slandering political revolutionary figures, a punishable offense under Chinese law. Gao was arrested in 2024 and held in a detention center for two years prior to his sentencing, and has been unable to see his wife or child. He plans to appeal.

On September 3, just two days before the opening of the 16th Gwangju Biennale, China withdrew from the exhibition, protesting the Gwangju Biennale Foundation’s decision to reinstate the title “Taiwan Pavilion” for Taiwan’s presentation. The fiasco dates back to June, when the foundation began referring to Taiwan’s project as “NTMoFA Pavilion”—using the acronym for the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, the organizing institution. The Chinese delegation stated that the restored title violates the “One China” principle, which South Korea formally adheres to.

In late September, Polish-born artist Alicja Kwade’s Waiting Pavilions (2024), an outdoor installation currently on display at Hong Kong’s Tai Kwun, was found vandalized. Set in Tai Kwun’s Prison Yard, the installation comprises several glass-brick cells along with boulders embedded in Monobloc chairs. One of the boulders had been separated from its chair and placed on the ground nearby. The work was restored and reopened to the public days later, while local police launched a criminal damage investigation.

HIROSHI SUGIMOTO ’s design for the new central garden of the Hirshhorn Museum, Washington, DC. Courtesy the Hirshhorn Museum.

Infrastructure

A new institution designed by Japanese architect Kengo Kuma is set to open in Singapore’s Orchard Road district in 2030. The 30-story design will feature an amphitheater, retail outlets, and offices, as well as a roughly 2,800-square-meter contemporary art museum run by the Tanoto Art Foundation.

The new Hirshhorn Sculpture Garden at the Smithsonian in Washington, DC, designed by Hiroshi Sugimoto, officially opened on October 31 after a four-year revitalization. The revamped garden, now reconnected to the rest of the Hirshhorn campus, features an expanded capacity for the display of some 60 classical and modernist sculptures.

article_text:
Obituary

Pipo Nguyen-duy, Beloved Photography Professor, Murdered at 64

"He took a lot of joy in his everyday life. He sought to make really beautiful photos, and strove to make the world a more beautiful place," said his former student.

Pipo Nguyen-duy, a beloved 64-year-old photography professor and the studio art department chair at Oberlin College in Ohio, and his wife, 56-year-old Tran Thi Phong, were fatally shot in their home on Wednesday, October 28.

Nguyen-duy's child and Phong's stepchild, 31-year-old Asia Nguyen-duy (birthname Daniel Jones), has been charged with their deaths and faces six counts of murder, one count of tampering with evidence, and four counts of felonious assault, per Oberlin Municipal Court records.

"I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community," Oberlin President Carmen Twillie Ambar wrote in a statement. "Pipo was beloved. During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography."
